newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro bourses ease, dollar strong against yen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro bourses ease, dollar strong against yen.

text.p: European bourses, their confidence sapped by another poor performance on Wall Street, eased again on Friday with investors opting to cash in profits from a recent bull run.

On currency markets, the dollar touched a 33-month high against the yen as traders said all reports from the Bank of Japan reinforced the belief that interest rates there would remain at record lows for some time.

Much attention was fixed on gloomy equity markets as analysts pondered whether the profit-taking of the last few days would turn into a stampede, halting the record-breaking run of recent weeks on bourses on both sides of the Atlantic.

London's FTSE 100 index slipped further below the psychologically important 4,000 mark on Friday as sentiment turned increasingly nervous and investors switched to the more attractive returns available on government bonds (gilts).
"Yields on gilts look set to break up above eight percent and that's becoming a real worry," said one dealer.
Weighed down by New York's drop overnight, the FTSE index lost more than 17 points in early business to 3,981.8, the lowest level of the month, before paring its losses.

"I don't think people are dramatically bearish. There's still a favourable technical background and cash flow remains quite good. That's why I don't think there's a huge amount of downside," one dealer said.
Some investors held back, awaiting U.S. figures due later in the day which would give clues on the health of the American economy and the prospects for interest rates.
The boom in markets has largely been fuelled by recent data showing subdued inflation in the powerful American economy and an optimistic outlook for rates.
In Washington, statistics on September durable goods will be released at 1230 GMT, home sales for September at 1400 GMT and a survey on consumer confidence at 1400 GMT.
In Frankfurt, shares fell 0.4 percent, depressed by weakness on Wall Street and in Tokyo's Nikkei index, which ended 1.25 percent down.
"Most things are just adjusting to the level on Wall Street," said one trader.
But some traders said the market was merely undergoing an expected consolidation after reaching record highs in the last few weeks and that the longer-term outlook was still positive.

French stocks also began the day slightly weaker, pressured by the Dow Jones industrial average's fall below 6,000 points and lower bond prices. But Rhone-Poulenc shares climbed 1.82 percent at 145.10 francs after the group announced a big rise in third-quarter net income.

The dollar, which was strengthening against the yen, was virtually unchanged against the mark despite comments in Brussels by Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing that under existing circumstances there could be no rate cut in Germany.
The U.S. currency hit a peak of 113.22 yen in early trade as the belief took hold that Japanese interest rates would remain low for some time.
That is encouraging further capital outflows from Japan in search of higher returns, traders said.

"The dollar is generally firmer today as we run into the weekend. And in perspective, we see the dollar's pullback this week as just a temporary correction," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
The U.S. currency's latest push higher against the yen was encpouraged by comments overnight from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Rubin reiterated the current Treasury position that a strong dollar was in the nation's interest and would help keep interest rates and inflation low.
CURRENCIES AT 0900 GMT
The dollar was trading at 1.5233 marks and 113.25 yen compared with 1.5230 and 112.90 yen on Thursday.
STOCKS AT 0900 GMT
London's FTSE 100 index was down 9.2 at 3990.2
Germany's DAX index was down 5.51 at 2672.92.
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 4.50 at 2,147.12.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $382.20 an ounce in the morning, compared with the close in London on Thursday of $383.10. Silver was unchanged at $4.91.
